accuracy-completeness.summary: Judge a Claude output on two axes before using it: completeness against the original request and accuracy against the primary source, without being swayed by fluency, formatting or Claude's own assessment.
points: Evaluate on two separate axes. Completeness: did the output cover everything the request asked for (every section, every metric, every entity)? Accuracy: does each claim match the source document or the real world? A polished output can fail either one.

Turn the original request into a checklist before you read the output (8 business units x 2 metrics = 16 cells; three policy requirements; ten obligations). Tick each item off against the source. This catches silent omissions and silent substitutions (6 months quietly becoming 12).

A claim that data is "not reported" or "not in the document" is itself a claim to verify. In long uploads Claude may miss a page rather than the data being absent; check the source before accepting a gap.
Fluency, consistent formatting, plausible-looking numbers and a sensible length are not evidence of correctness. They are what makes a wrong output dangerous.

Claude's own review of its output in the same conversation ("Is anything missing?", "Are you sure?", "Rate your confidence") is not an independent check; it tends to confirm what it just wrote. The exam guide is explicit that self-rated confidence is not an accuracy signal.

Spot checks estimate the error rate of what is present; they cannot detect what was left out. When the output is short enough to verify fully and the consequences are material, verify every item and scan the source (headings, table of contents) for topics the output never mentions.

Look for internal inconsistencies: percentages that cannot add up given how the data was collected, a respondent count that changes between paragraphs, a table that disagrees with the narrative. Any contradiction means at least one statement is wrong and the method is suspect.

For numbers, make the computation visible: ask Claude which rows, columns and years it used and how it calculated the result, or have it compute with its data analysis tool so counts are calculated rather than estimated. Then reconcile discrepancies before any figure is used.

Extra details that were not in the request (accrual rules, notice periods, industry norms) often come from Claude's general knowledge rather than your document. Ask Claude to point to the passage each one came from and remove anything it cannot source.

Re-running the request in a fresh chat checks consistency, not completeness: two runs can share the same omission or the same misreading. Use it as a supplement, never as the check against the source.

Anti-patterns the exam uses as distractors: accept because it reads well; accept because a sample of three was correct; ask Claude to list what it missed; check a total reconciles and infer the components are right; rescale or patch numbers whose derivation is unknown.

hallucinations-bias.summary: Recognize the signatures of hallucinated content, internal inconsistency and skewed framing in a Claude response, and know that specificity, confidence and consistency are not evidence of truth.
points: A hallucination is content that is factually wrong or not grounded in the provided context but presented as if it were. The help centre warns that Claude can "display quotes that may look authoritative or sound convincing, but are not grounded in fact" and can "write things that might look correct but are very mistaken".

The most convincing hallucinations are the most specific: named court cases with reporter citations, statute section numbers, report titles, statistics to one decimal place, quotations attributed to named executives. Precision is a red flag, not a credential.

Claude's training data has a cutoff, and without web search or an uploaded document it cannot know the contents of a recent report, regulation or announcement. Confident specifics about recent events produced with no source available are presumptively invented.

Claude can also hallucinate its own capabilities: it may produce links that do not work, or claim to have sent an email or created an external file when it has no such integration. Treat claims of external actions the same way as factual claims: verify.

Internal inconsistency is a hallucination signal: the market grows 12% in one paragraph and contracts in another; a table says 6 months and the conclusion says 4; percentages that cannot sum to 100% for multi-select data. At least one statement is wrong, and the whole output's method is suspect.

Skewed framing shows up as evaluative language that the numbers do not support ("aggressive" versus "competitive" pricing when the cheaper vendor is the one called aggressive), or as an output that rewards attributes not in the stated criteria (prestige of university or employer in a ranking that was supposed to be about frontline experience).

Bias survives anonymization. Removing names does not remove proxies such as institution prestige, employer size, postcode or writing style. Diagnose bias by comparing what the output rewards with what was asked for.

The remedy for skewed outputs is explicit criteria, traceable evidence and a human decision: re-run with a rubric limited to the stated criteria, require Claude to quote the evidence behind each score, and keep the shortlist or recommendation decision with a person. Anthropic does not endorse using models to make automated high-stakes decisions about people.

Consistency is not correctness. A repeatable ranking shows the skew is systematic; agreement between two runs shows the same error can be made twice; majority voting across three runs does not verify a single figure against the source.

Signs of a well-grounded output are the opposite of red flags: hedged language, a stated "gaps and limitations" section, a cell left blank with a note that the data could not be found, and an explicit "I don't have enough information". Anthropic's guidance encourages giving Claude permission to say it does not know.
Asking Claude whether it hallucinated or was biased, and accepting a no, is not detection. The model cannot reliably audit its own weighting, and a reassuring answer is not evidence.

When you find a hallucination or bias, use the thumbs-down feedback on the response; on Team and Enterprise plans feedback settings are managed by the admin. Feedback helps Anthropic but does not fix the output in front of you.

fact-checking.summary: Validate claims in a Claude output against primary sources using techniques that are independent of the model: quotes and citations you can open, independent recomputation, and second queries, never Claude's self-confirmation or self-rated confidence.
points: The gold standard is the primary source: the regulation text, the contract page, the published study, the official legislation site, the original spreadsheet. Confirm the number, its date, and what it measures (population, definition, market), because a correct figure about the wrong thing is still wrong.

For claims drawn from an uploaded document, ask Claude to quote the exact passage word for word and give the section and page it relied on, then open that page and read it. Direct quotes make the claim auditable; reading the source is the verification.

For claims from web search or Research mode, citations are pointers, not proof. Open each cited source and confirm it says what the summary says; the source can be out of date, about a different population, or misread. The help centre describes research citations as "easy-to-check", which is an invitation to check them.

For unsourced claims, run a fresh search or research query to find a primary source. If none can be found, remove the claim. Anthropic's guidance: have Claude find a supporting quote for each claim and retract any claim it cannot support.

For numbers Claude computed, ask which cells, columns and years it used, then recompute independently (a spreadsheet formula, a calculator). Code execution removes arithmetic error but not wrong-input error (wrong column, wrong start year, mixed currencies).

A second query in a fresh chat, or best-of-N comparison, is a useful cross-check for consistency: disagreement between runs flags a problem. Agreement does not prove correctness, because both runs can share the same error, so it supplements primary-source verification rather than replacing it.

Asking Claude "Are you sure?", "Can you confirm that clause exists?" or "Rate your confidence from 1 to 10" in the same conversation is not validation. Leading questions invite reaffirmation, and self-rated confidence does not track accuracy (exam guide sample 1).
Turning on web search and asking Claude to confirm its own citation confirms that a document exists, not that the cited section says what the draft claims. You still have to read the passage.
Repetition is not confirmation: several websites echoing the same statistic often trace back to one misquoted or outdated origin. Find the origin.
Softening an unverified claim ("roughly a fifth", "reports suggest") does not make it true. Either source it or remove it.

Fact-checking has a competence boundary. You can verify that a statute section exists and what it literally says; whether it permits a fee is a legal interpretation. When the remaining question is beyond your expertise, remove the claim or route it to a qualified reviewer.
Claude's own limitation notice applies: even with these techniques hallucinations are reduced, not eliminated. Always validate critical information, especially for high-stakes decisions.

human-review.summary: Decide when a Claude output must be reviewed by a qualified person or verified further before it is used, based on consequence, reversibility, audience, regulation and whether you can verify it yourself.
points: Human review is required when an output is external (customers, regulators, auditors, patients, the public), financial (payments, payouts, filings, reconciliations), legal (contracts, termination letters, statutory claims), medical, regulated, or irreversible (a sent email, a published description, a payroll run).

A separate trigger: anything you cannot personally verify. If the content requires expertise you do not have (clinical, legal, tax), a qualified person must review it regardless of how correct it reads to you.

These triggers are independent. Verifying every figure yourself satisfies the "can I verify it" test but does not waive review for an external, regulated record. An intercompany memo going to the auditors still goes through the controller sign-off after the analyst has checked the numbers.

Review must be by a person with the right competence and accountability: a clinician for patient instructions, legal for a termination letter or a statutory citation, a controller for a filing. The person who prompted is usually not that reviewer.

Low-risk outputs that do not need formal review: brainstorms the team will discuss anyway, summaries for people who were in the meeting, reformatting existing content, rewording your own message, notes for your own use. The audience can correct errors and the consequences are negligible.

Rephrasing is not risk-free. Turning a physician's bullets into plain language, or a supplier data sheet into marketing copy, can change a dose, a timing, an exception, or strengthen "supports" into "boosts". A correct source does not make the rewrite correct.

When full review of every output is infeasible, tier by risk: mandatory full review for regulated categories and anything carrying a health, safety, performance or compliance claim; sampled review for the rest; raise the sample rate when errors are found and lower it as quality proves stable.

Model self-review (a second pass by Claude checking the first) is a useful filter that can catch obvious errors, but it is not accountable review and cannot replace the human tier for high-consequence outputs.
A second run in a fresh chat is not a second reviewer. Agreement between two model outputs carries no accountability.
Disclaimers ("generated with AI assistance") and footers telling the reader to confirm with a professional do not substitute for review before distribution; they shift the burden to the audience.

Anthropic's own guidance is that users should not rely on Claude as a singular source of truth and should carefully scrutinize any high-stakes advice. The exam guide frames this as recognizing when human expertise, validation or escalation is required.
Escalation is also a competence decision: the Associate escalates complex or technical implementations to Claude Architects and Developers, and domain judgements to the relevant domain expert.

refine-outputs.summary: Treat a Claude draft as raw material: adapt it to the intended audience and purpose, correct what the model could not know, compare alternatives against explicit criteria, and remain the author of what goes out.
points: Adapting for an audience changes content, structure and tone, not just length. An engineering incident account becomes a customer update by leading with impact and next steps in plain language; shortening it to 200 words leaves it written for engineers.

For executives making a decision under time pressure, lead with the recommendation, the decision requested and the headline numbers; move methodology and supporting detail to an appendix. Density is the problem, not slide count; shrinking fonts does not help.

Ask for alternatives and compare them: two or three versions organized differently (by phase, by owner, by risk; six slides versus fourteen) evaluated against how the output will actually be used. Merge the best elements. The person chooses; asking Claude which version it prefers outsources a judgement that depends on knowing the room.

Give explicit criteria rather than adjectives. "Make it better", "warmer", "more executive" produce generic drift; "must cover security review, contract sign-off and payment setup, one owner per item" gives Claude something concrete to critique and revise against.
Give examples rather than descriptions of voice. To match a CEO's style, paste two or three of their previous messages; "make it sound like the CEO" yields generic executive-speak.

Fix what the model could not know: authority (a refund or discount the agent cannot offer), confirmed facts (whether roles will be affected), company policy, the specific customer's history. Claude has no way to know which claims are verified; do not delegate that with an instruction like "remove anything unverified".
Replace boilerplate with specifics. "We regret any inconvenience" reads as a template to a customer whose order was lost twice; refer to their situation and what you will actually do.

Keep the human as author and approver. Edit the draft, send it in your own words, and route it to the person whose name is on it (the CEO reads the all-hands aloud, the agent sends the email). Forwarding a raw draft with "AI-generated, needs a pass" hands the refinement to the busiest person.
Do not let a tone rewrite paper over a content problem, and do not escalate a commitment Claude invented to get it approved; correct the content first.
More is not better: doubling checklist items, adding data to prove rigour, or keeping every methodology slide reduces usability for the audience the output is meant to serve.

Inline editing in artifacts (highlight text and ask Claude to change just that part), editing an earlier message to branch a new version, and version history let you iterate on alternatives without losing earlier work.
Anti-patterns the exam uses as distractors: send as-is with an apology on top; shorten instead of adapt; "make it better" loops; let Claude pick its own best version; a disclaimer instead of an edit.

output-formats.summary: Choose the output format by who or what will consume it: an artifact for substantial content people will edit, reuse or share; an inline answer for quick one-off explanations; structured data (table, CSV, JSON, spreadsheet) when a tool is the next step; and curate accumulated material before formalizing it.
points: An artifact is "anything Claude makes for you that you'd put in front of someone": significant, self-contained content (typically more than about 15 lines) that you will edit, reuse or refer back to. Documents, slide outlines, tables, diagrams, dashboards and interactive tools all qualify; a project charter, meeting notes for a team, or a report fit here.

Inline responses suit quick answers you will read once and not reuse: a definition, a short explanation, a yes/no with reasoning. Creating an artifact for a two-sentence answer adds friction and clutters the workspace.

Structured data (a table or CSV with fixed columns, JSON, or an .xlsx file) is for outputs that another tool will ingest: a BI dashboard, a task tracker, a spreadsheet the analysts will filter. Ask for one row per record, consistent column names (ideally the consumer's exact import schema) and a controlled set of label values.

Prose and formatted reports are for people; they force manual re-keying when the next step is an import. JSON is for tools; readers should not be handed JSON. An image of a table cannot be filtered or sorted.

One source can need two formats. A meeting transcript becomes a notes artifact (decisions, actions, open questions) for the attendees and a CSV of action items (task, owner, due date, status) for the tracker. Choosing by consumer avoids losing content or retyping it.

Claude can create downloadable files (.docx, .xlsx, .pptx, .pdf, CSV) with its code execution and file creation feature, and artifacts export to Word, PDF, Markdown, Google Docs, PowerPoint. Pick the file type the recipient's tools use.
Format follows use, not setting: prep for a meeting is an inline explanation for you, not a slide; a definition is not a reference document just because it is about finance.

Curate before you formalize. When material has accumulated across chats (summaries, research findings, your notes), have Claude identify superseded and duplicated content for you to confirm, then organize by the deliverable's sections. Bundling everything into one artifact carries the noise forward.
Preserve provenance. Keep citations and source references in the curated document so the client or team can verify claims; stripping them "for cleanliness" destroys the ability to check.

Artifacts start private and can be published or shared; recipients can use a published artifact as a starting point for their own version. Inline editing (highlight and ask Claude to change that part) and version branching support iteration.

Anti-patterns the exam uses as distractors: a single long inline message to copy from; one monolithic artifact containing the report, the data and the notes; action items as paragraphs at the bottom of a document; JSON for human readers; a table embedded as an image; raw chat transcripts handed over instead of a curated deliverable.
